prompt: The AI provider's bill is counted in tokens, not in words or messages.
tells: counted in tokens, not in words
why: Models process text as tokens, small pieces of words, so usage and price are measured in them. Billing by tokens is the giveaway.
trap: A bigger model costs more per token, but the clue is the unit itself.

prompt: A developer sees the word 'unhappiness' split into 'un', 'happi' and 'ness' by the model's tokenizer.
why: Models don't read whole words; a tokenizer cuts text into common pieces. Those pieces are tokens.
trap: Embeddings come later; this is how the text is chopped up first.

prompt: The same sentence costs more to process in Thai than in English, because it breaks into more pieces.
why: Tokenizers are built mostly from English text, so other languages split into more tokens and cost more. That's about tokens.
trap: It isn't a model-size choice; the same model just sees more tokens.

prompt: The model struggles to count the letters in 'strawberry' because it sees chunks, not individual letters.
tells: it sees chunks, not individual letters
why: The model works on tokens, so single letters inside a word are hard for it to see. Token pieces explain the mistake.
trap: It is wrong, but the cause is how text is split, not invented facts.

prompt: The answer stopped mid-sentence because the request set a limit of 200 tokens for the reply.
tells: a limit of 200 tokens for the reply
why: Replies are also measured and capped in tokens. Hitting the output limit cuts the text off.
trap: The context window is the total the model can take in; this is a cap on the reply's tokens.

prompt: A rule of thumb says 100 tokens is about 75 English words.
why: Tokens are usually smaller than words, so there are more of them. Converting between the two is about tokens.
trap: Nothing is said about how much fits at once, so it isn't the context window.
